title: Implement streaming buffer-underrun wait loop (fix pauseIfUnderrun no-op)
description: BassPlayer.pauseIfUnderrun(bassStream:) is an immediate `return` followed by a giant commented-out block; the whole 'wait for more downloaded data before continuing' behavior is gone. In the shipping Obj-C app, keepRingBufferFilledInternal detected file underruns (isFileUnderrun set in MyFileReadProc when a read returns fewer bytes than requested) and entered a wait loop that: computes neededSize = localFileSize + bytesToBuffer(bitrate, recentDownloadSpeed), sleeps in 10ms ticks checking every 1s whether enough has downloaded / the song finished caching / it is the last temp-cached song, breaks the loop when satisfied, and calls moveToNextSong() in offline mode. Without this, streaming a song whose download can't keep up (or scrubbing near the end of the cached region) produces silence or an abrupt stop instead of pausing to buffer. 'Done' = playback pauses and resumes seamlessly when the download catches up, honors offline mode by skipping, and correctly terminates temp-cached/fully-cached songs — matching BassGaplessPlayer.m. Note BassStream already carries the dormant isWaiting/shouldBreakWaitLoop/shouldBreakWaitLoopForever fields for this, and bassGetOutputData already calls pauseIfUnderrun when bytesRead < length.
prompt: In Classes/Audio Engine/BassPlayer.swift, the method pauseIfUnderrun(bassStream:) is currently a no-op (`return` followed by a commented-out block) even though bassGetOutputData() calls it whenever BASS_ChannelGetData returns fewer bytes than requested. Reimplement the streaming buffer-underrun wait behavior that the shipping Objective-C version had in BassGaplessPlayer.m's keepRingBufferFilledInternal: when the current song is not fully cached, compute a needed size using Bass.bytesToBuffer(kiloBitrate:bytesPerSec:) with the current estimated bitrate and the StreamHandler's recentDownloadSpeedInBytesPerSec, then wait (checking the on-disk size roughly once per second, honoring shouldBreakWaitLoop/shouldBreakWaitLoopForever) until enough data has downloaded, the song is fully cached, or it is the last temp-cached song; in offline mode call moveToNextSong() instead of waiting. Use the existing BassStream.isWaiting / shouldBreakWaitLoop / shouldBreakWaitLoopForever flags and BassPlayer.waitLoopStream. Ensure this runs off the audio callback thread so it never blocks BASS output, and add integration tests that stream a partially-available file and assert playback pauses then resumes, plus a unit test for the buffering size calculation.

title: Fix inverted bounds guard in BassEqualizer.removeEqualizerValue
description: BassEqualizer.removeEqualizerValue(value:) starts with `guard value.arrayIndex >= eqValues.count else { return }`, which is inverted: it returns early (does nothing) for every VALID index (arrayIndex < count) and only proceeds when arrayIndex is out of range, where the subsequent `eqValues.remove(at: value.arrayIndex)` will crash. This method is invoked from EqualizerViewController.swift:435 when the user deletes an EQ band, so deleting an EQ point is currently a silent no-op (and a potential out-of-bounds crash). The Obj-C original (BassEqualizer.m removeEqualizerValue:) removes the value by object, removes its FX handle, and reindexes the remaining values. 'Done' = the guard is corrected (arrayIndex must be < count), the FX is removed via BASS_ChannelRemoveFX only when the EQ is active, the value and handle are removed, and remaining values' arrayIndex are re-sequenced, matching the Obj-C behavior.
prompt: In Classes/Audio Engine/BassEqualizer.swift, removeEqualizerValue(value:) has an inverted guard `guard value.arrayIndex >= eqValues.count else { return }` that makes deleting an EQ band a no-op for valid indices and an out-of-bounds crash otherwise. Compare with the Objective-C original in BassGaplessPlayer/BassEqualizer.m (removeEqualizerValue:), which removes the value by identity, calls BASS_ChannelRemoveFX(channel, value.handle) when the EQ is active, removes the handle from eqHandles, and re-sequences the arrayIndex of the remaining eqValues. Fix the guard so it correctly bounds-checks (arrayIndex must be within range), remove the value and its FX handle, and reindex remaining values under eqValuesLock. Add a unit test that adds several EQ values then removes a middle one and asserts the count, remaining arrayIndex ordering, and that no crash occurs, plus a UI test that adds and deletes an EQ point in the equalizer editor.

title: Handle next-song stream creation failure at song end (bassFailedToCreateNextStream parity)
description: When a song ends and the next song's stream cannot yet be created (e.g. it hasn't downloaded far enough), the shipping app set isNextSongStreamFailed and invoked the delegate bassFailedToCreateNextStreamForIndex:, which retried playing that index once the download had informed the player to start (see iSubBassGaplessPlayerDelegate.m). The Swift port has no equivalent: songEnded() and prepareNextStream() simply attempt prepareStream and, on failure, do nothing, so at a gapless boundary with a not-yet-ready next song playback can silently stall. The commented-out isNextSongStreamFailed hook still exists in BassCallbacks.swift. 'Done' = when the next stream fails to prepare at end-of-song, the player retries that index when appropriate (mirroring the streamManager handler / isDelegateNotifiedToStartPlayback logic in the Obj-C delegate), so the playlist advances rather than hanging.
prompt: In Classes/Audio Engine/BassPlayer.swift, prepareNextStream() and songEnded(bassStream:) do not handle the case where the next song's stream cannot be created at a gapless boundary because it hasn't downloaded far enough. The shipping Objective-C app handled this via BassGaplessPlayer's isNextSongStreamFailed flag plus the delegate method bassFailedToCreateNextStreamForIndex: in iSubBassGaplessPlayerDelegate.m, which re-triggered playback of that index when the song's StreamHandler was not downloading or had already notified the player to start. Reproduce this: detect when prepareStream for the next song returns nil at song end, and retry the next index through PlayQueue when appropriate so the playlist advances instead of stalling in silence. Add an integration test that simulates a next song that becomes streamable slightly after the current song ends and asserts playback continues to it.

title: Restore end-of-playlist stop/cleanup safety net in bassGetOutputData
description: In the Obj-C bassGetOutputData:, when the ring buffer drained 0 bytes, the current stream's BASS channel was inactive, and the song was fully/temp cached, the player set isPlaying=NO, forced songEnded if it hadn't been called, posted SongPlaybackEnded, ran cleanup on the main thread, and asked the delegate to retry the current index — a safety net for the final song and for cases where the end sync didn't fire. The Swift bassGetOutputData only calls the (currently no-op) pauseIfUnderrun and returns bytesRead; it relies solely on the BASS_SYNC_END callback. If the mixer goes inactive at the end of the queue, the Swift player can leave isPlaying=true and the audio session active with no cleanup. 'Done' = at true end-of-playback (no current stream / inactive channel with no more data) the player stops, deactivates the session, posts SongPlaybackEnded, and cleans up, matching the Obj-C safety path.
prompt: In Classes/Audio Engine/BassPlayer.swift, bassGetOutputData(buffer:length:) lacks the end-of-playback safety net that the Objective-C bassGetOutputData: had in BassGaplessPlayer.m. Add handling for when there is no current stream, or the current stream's BASS channel is no longer active and no bytes were read and the song is fully/temp cached: set isPlaying=false, ensure songEnded ran, post Notifications.songPlaybackEnded, run cleanup() on the main thread, and advance/retry via PlayQueue so the player stops cleanly at the end of the playlist and deactivates the audio session. Add an integration test that plays the last song in a queue to completion and asserts the player stops, the session deactivates, and bassFreed/songPlaybackEnded notifications fire.

title: Fix downloadedSongs(serverId:) to filter by serverId

title: Fix malformed batch download-queue insert SQL

title: Eliminate GRDB reentrancy (nested pool.read inside pool.write)
description: Several write transactions perform reads through separate Store helpers that open their own pool.read/pool.write, which GRDB DatabasePool does not permit (database access is not reentrant) and can deadlock or throw. BookmarkStore.addBookmark runs inside pool.write but calls the `nextLocalPlaylistId`/`nextBookmarkId` computed properties (each does pool.read) and playQueue.song(...). DownloadsStore.deleteDownloadedSongs(serverId:level:), deleteDownloadedSongs(downloadedTagArtist:) and (downloadedTagAlbum:) call self.song(serverId:id:) (pool.read) inside their pool.write closures. Done = perform these lookups against the passed `db` handle within the same transaction instead of re-entering the pool.
prompt: Fix GRDB reentrancy hazards in the store layer. In `Classes/Models/Data Store/BookmarkStore.swift`, `addBookmark(...)` runs inside `pool.write { db in ... }` but calls `nextLocalPlaylistId` and `nextBookmarkId` (each of which opens its own `pool.read`), which is non-reentrant on a DatabasePool. In `Classes/Models/Data Store/DownloadsStore.swift`, `deleteDownloadedSongs(serverId:level:)` (~line 641), `deleteDownloadedSongs(downloadedTagArtist:)` (~line 673) and `deleteDownloadedSongs(downloadedTagAlbum:)` (~line 695) call `self.song(serverId:id:)` (which opens `pool.read`) inside their `pool.write` closures. Refactor so all reads use the in-transaction `db` handle (add `static`/private helpers that take `db` and compute MAX(id) or fetch the Song directly), avoiding any nested pool access. Add a unit/integration test that exercises addBookmark and each delete path to confirm they complete without deadlock/throw and produce correct results.

title: Fix inverted guard in DownloadQueue.stop() that makes it a no-op while downloading
description: DownloadQueue.stop() begins with `guard !isDownloading else { return }`, which returns early precisely when a download IS in progress, so the cancel/cleanup code never runs during active downloading. The Obj-C original does the opposite: `if (!self.isQueueDownloading) return;` (ISMSCacheQueueManager.m -stopDownloadQueue) — it returns only when NOT downloading. Because removeCurrentSong() and clear() both call stop(), cancelling the current download, clearing the queue, and entering offline mode all fail to actually cancel the in-flight stream handler. Done = invert the guard to `guard isDownloading else { return }` and verify removeCurrentSong/clear/didEnterOfflineMode actually cancel the active handler.

Verify the callers removeCurrentSong(), clear(), and didEnterOfflineMode() now genuinely halt the active download. Add a unit/integration test that starts a download, calls stop(), and asserts the handler is cancelled and isDownloading becomes false.

title: Restore download bandwidth throttling / rate limiting in StreamHandler
description: The Obj-C ISMSNSURLSessionStreamHandler throttles download bandwidth in didReceiveData: once past the start-limiting threshold it computes maxBytesPerIntervalForBitrate (cell vs wifi) and sleeps the connection thread to cap throughput, controlled by isEnableRateLimiting. The Swift StreamHandler's urlSession(_:dataTask:didReceive:) has no throttling at all — it only updates a `throttlingDate` that is never used, and the helper functions maxBytesPerInterval/maxBytesPerIntervalCell/maxBytesPerIntervalWifi plus the `isThrottleLoggingEnabled` flag are dead code. This means next-song pre-caching and manual downloads consume full bandwidth, competing with the currently-playing stream and cellular data limits. Done = implement interval-based throttling mirroring the Obj-C logic (respecting cell vs wifi, only after minBytesToStartLimiting), wired to a rate-limiting flag, without blocking the main thread.
prompt: In Classes/Models/Stream Handlers/StreamHandler.swift, download bandwidth throttling was never ported. The Objective-C original Classes/Models/Stream Handlers/ISMSNSURLSessionStreamHandler.m in URLSession:dataTask:didReceiveData: throttles by computing maxBytesPerIntervalForBitrate (different caps for cellular vs wifi) and sleeping when bytesTransferred exceeds the allowed amount per ISMSThrottleTimeInterval, gated by isEnableRateLimiting and only after ISMSMinBytesToStartLimiting. The Swift port has the helper functions maxBytesPerInterval/maxBytesPerIntervalCell/maxBytesPerIntervalWifi and a throttlingDate property but never applies them. Implement the throttle in the didReceive data delegate (using the existing helpers, checking SceneDelegate.shared.isWifi for the cell/wifi cap), ensuring it runs off the main thread since the URLSession delegate queue is a background queue. Add unit tests for the maxBytesPerInterval math and an integration test asserting throughput is capped for a background/pre-cache download.

title: Reimplement partial pre-cache of the next song
description: The Obj-C stream handler supported partial pre-caching of the next song: while caching a non-current song it would download up to ISMSNumBytesToPartialPreCache (secondsToPartialPrecache worth) and then sleep the download (partialPrecacheSleep loop), controlled by the isPartialCacheNextSong setting, resuming when needed (see ISMSNSURLSessionStreamHandler.m didReceiveData partial pre-cache block and ISMSStreamManager/ISMSCacheQueueManager delegate handling of ISMSStreamHandlerPartialPrecachePaused). The Swift port has none of this — there is no partialPrecacheSleep, no secondsToPartialPrecache, and no isPartialCacheNextSong setting anywhere; only a coarse isNextSongCacheEnabled (full pre-cache) exists. Result: the app either fully downloads the next song or nothing, losing the bandwidth-friendly partial pre-cache behavior. Done = port the partial pre-cache pause/resume mechanism and the isPartialCacheNextSong setting, or make a deliberate, documented decision to drop it.
prompt: The Objective-C iSub could partially pre-cache the next song and then pause the download until playback needed more, controlled by the isPartialCacheNextSong setting. The Swift port (Classes/Models/Stream Handlers/StreamHandler.swift and StreamManager.swift) dropped this entirely and only has a full-next-song cache via settings.isNextSongCacheEnabled. Port the partial pre-cache behavior: add the isPartialCacheNextSong setting, download up to the partial threshold for a non-current, non-temp song, then pause the URLSession task and resume it when the song becomes current or the stream queue advances, without blocking the main thread. Add unit/integration tests verifying the download pauses at the partial threshold and resumes correctly.

title: Fix playback start threshold: buffers 60s instead of 10s
description: In StreamHandler.urlSession(_:dataTask:didReceive:) the decision to notify the delegate to start playback uses minBytesToStartLimiting(kiloBitrate:) which is 60 seconds of audio (line 315 / helper at 440). The Obj-C original starts playback at ISMSMinBytesToStartPlayback = 10 seconds (ISMSStreamHandler.h define; ISMSNSURLSessionStreamHandler.m uses it in didReceiveData). The Swift file even defines an adaptive minBytesToStartPlayback(kiloBitrate:bytesPerSec:) (lines 460-495) and a minimumBytesToStartPlayback (10s), but neither is called for the start-playback gate. Result: songs take far longer to begin playing (must buffer ~60s) than in the shipping app. Done = gate start-playback on the 10s/adaptive threshold, not the 60s limiting threshold, and reserve minBytesToStartLimiting solely for throttling.
prompt: In Classes/Models/Stream Handlers/StreamHandler.swift, the urlSession(_:dataTask:didReceive:) method starts playback once totalBytesTransferred exceeds minBytesToStartLimiting(kiloBitrate:), which is 60 seconds of audio — but the Objective-C original (Classes/Models/Stream Handlers/ISMSStreamHandler.h define ISMSMinBytesToStartPlayback = 10 seconds, used in ISMSNSURLSessionStreamHandler.m didReceiveData) starts after only ~10 seconds. The Swift file already defines minimumBytesToStartPlayback (10s) and an adaptive minBytesToStartPlayback(kiloBitrate:bytesPerSec:) that are currently unused. Change the start-playback gate to use the adaptive/10-second threshold and keep minBytesToStartLimiting only for the (separately fixed) throttling logic. Add a unit test verifying the start-playback byte threshold corresponds to ~10s at a given bitrate, and an integration test asserting streamHandlerStartPlayback fires early.

title: Create XCUITest target with launch-argument test mode and deterministic stubbed server
description: No UI-test target exists in iSub.xcodeproj (grep of project.pbxproj shows no com.apple.product-type.bundle.ui-testing target; only the iSubTESTING app target and ENABLE_TESTABILITY). There is also no launch-argument handling anywhere (no ProcessInfo/CommandLine parsing outside main.swift), so tests cannot force a known state. 'Done' means: (1) add an 'iSubUITests' XCUITest bundle target wired to the iSub app as TEST_TARGET_NAME; (2) add launch-argument/environment parsing early in AppDelegate.application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:) and SceneDelegate for flags like -UITEST 1, -RESET_STATE 1 (wipe DB + caches + UserDefaults for a clean first-run), -MODE online|offline|jukebox, and -FIXTURES <name>; (3) provide a deterministic offline Subsonic backend by registering a custom URLProtocol (the AsyncAPILoader session uses URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral, so protocolClasses can be injected in test mode) or a localhost fixture HTTP server that returns recorded Subsonic XML/JSON responses and streamable audio, so no real network/server is required; (4) seed a fake configured server so first-run setup can be bypassed when a test needs an already-logged-in state. This is the prerequisite for every other UITest finding.
prompt: In the iSub iOS project (iSub.xcodeproj), there is currently no UI-test target and no way to run the app deterministically offline. Add an XCUITest bundle target named 'iSubUITests' configured against the iSub app target. Then add launch-argument/environment handling early in Classes/Main/AppDelegate.swift (application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)) and Classes/Main/SceneDelegate.swift to support flags: -UITEST (enable test mode), -RESET_STATE (wipe the GRDB database, on-disk caches, and UserDefaults for a clean first-run), -MODE online|offline|jukebox, and -FIXTURES <name> (select a recorded response set). Implement a deterministic backend for test mode by registering a custom URLProtocol into the ephemeral URLSession used by Classes/Models/Async Loaders/AsyncAPILoader.swift (see its sharedSession/defaultSharedSession) that returns recorded Subsonic API responses and a small local audio file for streaming, so tests never hit a real server. Provide a helper to seed an already-configured server so tests can skip first-run setup. Write one smoke XCUITest that launches the app in each mode and asserts the app reaches its root UI, and document the launch-argument contract in the test target.

title: Pin ProgressHUD dependency to a tag/commit instead of a moving branch
description: In project.pbxproj the ProgressHUD SwiftPM dependency uses requirement kind = branch, branch = einsteinx2 against a personal fork (github.com/einsteinx2/ProgressHUD). Every other dependency uses upToNextMajorVersion. A branch requirement means `swift package update` can silently pull new HEAD of that branch, changing behavior of the app's HUD/overlays with no version bump; it is also a supply-chain/reproducibility risk for an App Store release. Package.resolved currently pins revision 3088718b... but the requirement itself will move. Done = the requirement is changed to a version tag or an exact commit (kind = revision), matching the intended pinned commit.
prompt: In iSub.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj the ProgressHUD Swift package (XCRemoteSwiftPackageReference "ProgressHUD", repositoryURL https://github.com/einsteinx2/ProgressHUD) is pinned by `kind = branch; branch = einsteinx2`, unlike all other dependencies which use upToNextMajorVersion. Change this requirement to pin an exact commit (kind = revision, revision = the commit currently in Package.resolved, 3088718b42305f5061b7d370c4fc44b98739af0c) or a proper version tag, so `swift package update` cannot silently move it. Update Package.resolved accordingly, resolve packages, and confirm the app still builds. Verify no other dependency uses a branch requirement.
